scenario: WIBTA for lying to my brother for the rest of our lives about having a disorder? | My brother who is 2 years younger than me has Aspberger's. We have known for years but it's not something that we talk about in my family because my brother is embarrassed of it in a way. He is EXTREMELY smart and always has been. He excels in math and physics and everything in between. He is going to college and taking hard classes that he does well in. Lately, he has been depressed. More than depressed. A couple of months ago, he tried to take his own life by getting drunk and swallowing a bottle of acetaminophen. He and I are extremely close and he only talks to me. He called me in a panic hours after doing this and I took him to the hospital. He went to outpatient treatment after getting discharged from inpatient. The nurse had called me and asked if my brother was diagnosed with autism ever because he shows some clear signs. I talked to my brother about it today and he is still somewhat denying that he has autism. My brother loves me to death and I love him just as much. He has always looked up to me. I can't imagine a world without him. He loves how much more alike we get as we get older. He constantly says it with a big smile on his face. I have tried to talk to him about his autism and how he shouldn't be ashamed and he should own that about himself because some people don't even realize he has bad communication skills and he's so damn smart. Occasionally, his bad communication skills are very apparent and his disorder is obvious in other ways as well. I try to tell him that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Aspberger's but it doesn't do much for him when I say that. I feel if I tell my brother I have Aspberger's as well he would learn to love it and not deny it anymore, possibly helping himself. Would I be an asshole if I live a lie for the rest of my life to make my brother feel he's not alone and possibly help him move forward in life?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to lie to my brother about having Asperger's syndrome. Let me start by understanding the situation better. My brother is 2 years younger than me and has Asperger's. We've known about it for years, but it's not something we talk about much in our family because he's embarrassed. He's extremely smart, excels in math and physics, and is doing well in college. Lately, he's been really depressed, even to the point of attempting suicide a couple of months ago. He called me in a panic, and I took him to the hospital. After that, he went through outpatient treatment. Recently, a nurse asked me if my brother was diagnosed with autism because she noticed some signs. I talked to him about it today, but he's still denying it. He loves me a lot, and I love him too. We're very close, and he looks up to me. I can't imagine life without him. He's always saying how much we're alike as we get older, with a big smile on his face. I've tried talking to him about his Asperger's, telling him he shouldn't be ashamed and that he should embrace it because some people don't even realize he has communication difficulties. He's so smart, but sometimes his communication skills are really apparent, and his disorder is noticeable in other ways too. I mentioned that people say Mark Zuckerberg and Steve Jobs have Asperger's, but that didn't help much. Now, I'm considering telling him that I have Asperger's too. I think this might help him accept his diagnosis and not deny it anymore, which could help him move forward in life. But I'm wondering if lying about it would make me a asshole. Is this the right thing to do? First, I need to consider the potential benefits of lying. If I tell him I have Asperger's, he might feel less alone and more accepted. It could help him embrace his diagnosis and reduce his feelings of shame. Since we're so close, knowing that I have it too might make him feel more connected to me and less isolated. On the other hand, lying could have serious consequences. If he finds out I lied, he might feel betrayed, which could damage our relationship. Trust is crucial, especially given how close we are. Also, lying about having a disorder could be seen as trivializing the condition, especially if I don't actually have it. It might send the wrong message about the importance of honesty and authenticity. I should also think about why he's denying his diagnosis. Maybe he's struggling with self-acceptance or facing societal stigma. Instead of lying, perhaps there's another way to support him. I could continue to encourage him to embrace his strengths and help him see that having Asperger's doesn't define him but is just one part of who he is. Another approach might be to seek professional help or support groups where he can talk about his feelings with others who understand. This might provide him with the acceptance and understanding he needs without me having to lie. I also need to consider the ethical implications. Lying, even with good intentions, can have unintended negative effects. It's important to weigh the potential benefits against the risks. If the lie helps him in the short term but could cause harm in the long term, it might not be worth it. In conclusion, while the intention to help my brother is good, lying about having Asperger's might not be the best approach. It could lead to betrayal and damage trust. Instead, focusing on open communication, support, and seeking appropriate resources might be a better way to help him accept and embrace his diagnosis.
